This course is about one practical skill: **knowing when a pregnant woman, a new mother, a newborn or a young child needs a health worker, and getting them there in time**. It is not a medical course. It will not teach you to diagnose or treat anyone, and it never gives medicine doses. What it gives you is health literacy: the ability to understand health information, recognise danger, ask good questions at the clinic and act quickly.
This course does not replace a health worker

Everything here supports, and never replaces, care from a trained health worker at a clinic, primary health care centre or hospital. If you see a danger sign, do not wait to finish a lesson or to ask friends on WhatsApp. Go to a health facility.
What the World Health Organization tells us

The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes fact sheets on maternal and newborn deaths. Its maternal mortality fact sheet estimates that about **260,000 women died in 2023** from causes linked to pregnancy and childbirth. That is **over 700 women every day**, and about **92% of these deaths happened in low and lower-middle income countries**. WHO also says plainly that **most maternal deaths are preventable**, because the health care solutions are well known.
According to WHO, five complications account for about **75% of all maternal deaths**:

Newborns: the first week matters most

WHO's newborn mortality fact sheet reports that **2.3 million newborns died in their first 28 days in 2022**, and that **about 75% of newborn deaths happen in the first week of life**. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest newborn death rate in the world, at about 27 deaths per 1,000 live births. The main causes are being born too early, problems during birth (such as the baby not breathing well), infections and birth defects.

This is why the hours and days right after birth get so much attention in this course. A baby who stops feeding well, becomes floppy, breathes with difficulty, has a fever, has fits or feels cold needs care quickly.
Where time is lost
When a woman or child dies from a complication that could have been treated, time has usually been lost somewhere along the way. It helps to think of three places where this happens:
Three places time is lost
Danger sign appears
Delay deciding at home
Delay on the road
Delay at the facility
Treatment
Health literacy shortens the first delay, and planning shortens the second.
**Deciding at home.** Nobody recognises the danger sign, or the family waits for a husband, mother-in-law or pastor to give permission, or tries home remedies first.
**Getting there.** There is no transport at night, no money for the fare, or nobody knows which facility can handle the problem.
**At the facility.** The facility lacks staff, blood or supplies, or the woman arrives without her records and the staff must start from zero.

You cannot fix every problem at the facility, but you can do a lot about the first two. Knowing the danger signs removes the first delay. A written plan for transport, money and the right facility removes much of the second. Carrying the antenatal card or child health card helps with the third.
Worked example: finding the delays in a real-life story
For example, Ngozi is 34 weeks pregnant and lives about 40 minutes by road from the general hospital. One evening she has a severe headache and says her eyes are blurry.
Her sister says it is probably tiredness and suggests she sleeps. This is a possible **delay at home**: a severe headache with blurred vision is a warning sign of pre-eclampsia.
Her husband is travelling, and she does not want to go without his permission. Another **delay at home**.
At 10 pm they look for a car. The usual driver is not answering. This is a **delay on the road**.
They finally arrive at midnight, without her antenatal card. Staff must ask many questions before they can see her history. This adds a **delay at the facility**.

Each delay was avoidable: knowing the sign, agreeing in advance that she can go without waiting for permission, saving a second driver's number, and keeping the card in her bag. These are exactly the habits this course builds.

Antenatal care: the eight contacts and what happens at each

**Antenatal care (ANC)** is the care a woman receives from a skilled health worker during pregnancy. In 2016 WHO updated its guidance and now recommends **a minimum of eight contacts** during pregnancy, instead of the older model of four visits. WHO says that moving to eight contacts can reduce deaths of babies around the time of birth and improve women's experience of care.
The word **contact** is used instead of visit because a contact means real, active interaction with a health worker, not just collecting a card or waiting in a queue.
The WHO timing

WHO recommends that the **first contact happens in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy**, with later contacts at **20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks**. Notice that the contacts become closer together near the end, when problems such as high blood pressure are more likely to appear.

Only take medicines and supplements given or approved by your health worker. Do not buy pregnancy medicines on your own from a chemist or a hawker, and do not copy what a friend was given. This course will never tell you how much of any medicine to take.
Planning your dates

Many women start antenatal care late, sometimes after 20 weeks, because they feel well or because the clinic is far. The first contact in the first 12 weeks is important because it allows the dating scan to be planned in time, starts iron and folic acid early, and gives the health worker a baseline for blood pressure and weight.
Worked example: writing out all eight contact dates
For example, Halima had her first antenatal contact on Tuesday 3 March 2026, when the health worker told her she was 11 weeks pregnant. She wants all her contact dates in her phone calendar.
Week 20 is 9 weeks after week 11. 9 weeks is 63 days. 3 March plus 63 days is **Tuesday 5 May 2026**.
Week 26 is 6 weeks later: **Tuesday 16 June 2026**.
Week 30 is 4 weeks later: **Tuesday 14 July 2026**. Week 34 is 4 weeks later: **Tuesday 11 August 2026**.
Weeks 36, 38 and 40 are every 2 weeks: **25 August, 8 September and 22 September 2026**.
She adds each date to her phone calendar with a reminder two days before, and writes them on the inside cover of her antenatal card.

Halima has seven more dates planned, making eight contacts in total. If the clinic gives her a different date, she follows the clinic, because the health worker may adjust the schedule for her situation.
Making each contact count
Take your antenatal card or booklet to every visit, and any scan or test results.
Write down questions before you go. For example: What was my blood pressure? Is my blood level okay? When is my next visit?
Tell the health worker about anything new: headaches, bleeding, fever, pain, swelling, or worries about the baby's movements.
Ask what your blood pressure and test results mean, and write them down.
Before leaving, confirm the date of your next contact.

Antenatal care is also where you get information about birth planning, breastfeeding and family planning after birth. If your partner or a family member can come with you to at least one visit, they will hear the same information and be better prepared to help.

Keep all your antenatal records together in one plastic sleeve or envelope: the card, scan reports and test results. Take a clear photo of each page on your phone after every contact. If the card is lost or you go to a different facility in an emergency, these photos help the staff understand your pregnancy quickly.
If you missed a visit
Go as soon as you can. Do not wait for the next scheduled date or feel ashamed to return. A late contact is far better than no contact.

Pregnancy brings many changes that are uncomfortable but usually normal, such as tiredness or mild nausea. A **danger sign** is different. It is a sign that something may be seriously wrong and that the woman needs a health worker **now**, not tomorrow and not after a home remedy. In this lesson we focus on the signs linked to the main causes of maternal death described by WHO.
High blood pressure: pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

WHO's pre-eclampsia fact sheet describes it as high blood pressure (140/90 or more) with protein in the urine, **after 20 weeks of pregnancy**. Without treatment it can lead to **eclampsia (fits)**, damage to the kidneys, liver and brain, separation of the placenta, early birth, and death of the mother or baby. The warning signs WHO lists are:
**Severe headache** that does not go away.
**Problems with vision**, such as blurred vision or seeing spots.
**Pain in the upper belly**.
**Fits (convulsions)**, which mean eclampsia and are an emergency.

WHO notes that the risk is higher in first pregnancies, twin or multiple pregnancies, women with obesity, and women who already have high blood pressure, diabetes or kidney disease. This is one reason blood pressure is checked at every antenatal contact.
Bleeding and infection

WHO identifies **severe bleeding, mostly after childbirth**, as a leading cause of maternal death, and **infections, usually after childbirth**, as another. So the danger signs continue after the baby is born. Heavy bleeding, fever, or feeling very unwell in the days after birth are reasons to go immediately.

The rule: danger sign means go now

When a danger sign appears, the safest response is always the same: **go to a health facility that can handle emergencies, immediately, day or night**. Do not wait to see if it gets better. Do not give herbal mixtures or medicines bought on the way. Bring the antenatal card. If possible, call the facility on the way so they are ready.

Which facility? For a danger sign, choose a facility that can manage emergencies, such as a general hospital, rather than the nearest small health post, if both can be reached. A small health post may need to send the woman on to a hospital, which adds a second journey. Ask at your antenatal contact which hospital your clinic refers emergencies to, and write it on your danger sign card.
If a woman is having a fit

Keep her away from fire, water and sharp objects, lie her on her side once the fit allows, do not put anything in her mouth, and get her to a facility immediately. Eclampsia needs treatment that only a health facility can give.
Worked example: a phone call from a neighbour

For example, Blessing's neighbour Amaka, 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby, calls at 7 pm. She says she has had a bad headache since morning and her eyes feel blurry. She asks whether she should take paracetamol and lie down.
Blessing checks the signs: severe headache that has lasted all day, blurred vision, after 20 weeks, first pregnancy. These match the WHO warning signs of pre-eclampsia.
She does not suggest any medicine. She says: "These are danger signs. You need your blood pressure checked tonight."
She asks Amaka who can take her and helps her call the driver on her emergency list.
She reminds her to bring her antenatal card and phone charger.
Amaka reaches the hospital within the hour, where her blood pressure is checked. Blessing did not diagnose or treat; she recognised the signs and removed the delay at home.
After the birth

Many families relax once the baby arrives, but WHO's figures show that bleeding and infection after birth are major killers. WHO's postnatal care recommendations also include screening mothers for **depression and anxiety**. If a new mother seems unable to cope, cannot sleep even when the baby sleeps, or speaks about harming herself or the baby, she needs a health worker's help quickly. This is a health problem, not a weakness.

Labour often starts at night, on a weekend or when the person you rely on is away. Families who decide everything in advance save precious time. A **birth and emergency plan** is a short written plan that answers five questions: **where** the baby will be born, **who** will go with the mother, **how** she will get there, **how much** it will cost, and **what** to do if something goes wrong.
Why the place of birth matters

WHO stresses that **all births should be attended by skilled health professionals**, because timely management and treatment can make the difference between life and death. Its maternal mortality fact sheet notes that about 99% of births in high-income countries have a skilled attendant, compared with about 73% in low-income countries. A skilled attendant is a trained midwife, nurse or doctor who can manage a normal birth and recognise and handle complications, or refer quickly.

WHO also recommends that mother and baby receive care in the facility for **at least 24 hours after birth**. Plan for this: bring enough items for a day or more, and do not arrange to leave a few hours after the birth just to save money.

Ask the facility, not the market

Ask at your antenatal contact what the facility charges and what you must bring. Some services are free or subsidised in public facilities. Use their answer, not a neighbour's guess, to set your saving target.
The first hour: essential newborn care
WHO lists essential care every newborn should receive. Knowing it helps you understand what the midwife is doing and support it:
**Warmth**: dry the baby and place them skin-to-skin on the mother's chest, covered with a cloth. Babies lose heat very quickly.
**Early breastfeeding**: WHO recommends starting breastfeeding **within one hour of birth**, and giving only breast milk for the first six months.
**Clean cord and skin care**: keep the cord stump clean and dry. Do not put anything on it unless a health worker tells you to.
**Checks and vaccines**: the baby is examined, and vaccines given at birth are recorded on the child's card.
Do not apply substances to the cord
Putting ash, dung, oil or any home mixture on the cord can bring infection. WHO's newborn guidance calls for hygienic cord and skin care. Follow your health worker's instructions only.
If labour starts somewhere unexpected

Even with a good plan, labour can come early or quickly. The plan still helps: the bag is ready, the drivers are saved and the money is set aside. Ask your health worker at an antenatal contact exactly when you should leave for the facility once labour begins, and leave early rather than late if the facility is far away. If a danger sign appears at any time, follow the plan for emergencies and go to the bigger hospital directly if it can be reached safely.

The weeks after birth are called the **postnatal period**. WHO's newborn fact sheet reports that most newborn deaths happen in the **first week of life**, and its maternal fact sheet shows bleeding and infection after birth are leading causes of maternal death. Yet WHO has also reported that **more than 3 in 10 women and babies do not receive postnatal care in the first days after birth**. This lesson makes sure your family is not one of them.
The WHO postnatal contacts

In 2022 WHO recommended care in a facility for **at least 24 hours after birth**, followed by **at least three more postnatal check-ups in the first six weeks**: between **48 and 72 hours**, between **7 and 14 days**, and during **week six**. These can be at the facility or through home visits, depending on what your area offers.

Newborn danger signs
WHO advises families to seek care promptly if a newborn has any of these signs. Learn them by heart and teach them to everyone who holds the baby:
**Feeding problems**: the baby is not feeding well or has stopped feeding.
**Reduced activity**: the baby is unusually sleepy, floppy or moves only when stimulated, or not at all.
**Difficult breathing**.
**Fever**, or the baby **feels cold**.
**Fits or convulsions**.
A newborn with a danger sign goes today

Do not wait for the next scheduled check. Keep the baby warm against the mother's skin, keep offering the breast if the baby can feed, and go to a facility immediately with the baby's card. Do not give herbal mixtures, glucose water or medicines on the way.
Breastfeeding: the basics that matter here

WHO recommends that babies start breastfeeding **within one hour of birth**, receive **only breast milk for the first six months** (no water, no glucose water, no herbal drinks, no formula unless a health worker advises it), and continue breastfeeding **up to two years or beyond**. In the postnatal period, the most useful thing a family can do is protect the mother's time and rest so she can feed often, and bring her to the checks where health workers help with attachment and positioning. Our companion course on community nutrition covers feeding from six months onwards in detail.
Tradition and the first milk

The thick yellowish first milk is part of breast milk and is good for the baby. If relatives suggest throwing it away or giving water first, kindly explain that WHO recommends breast milk only, starting in the first hour.
The mother after birth

Families often focus on the baby and forget the mother. Remember the danger signs from Module 1: heavy bleeding, fever, severe headache, fits. Add her mood. WHO now includes screening for postnatal depression and anxiety. A mother who feels hopeless, cannot sleep even when she can, or cannot care for herself or the baby should be taken to a health worker. Practical help, such as cooking, washing and taking turns with the baby at night, protects her recovery.

The postnatal contacts are a good time to ask a health worker about family planning options that are suitable while breastfeeding, so the next pregnancy comes when the family is ready.

Identify signs of dehydration and explain how ORS works
Explain why a child with fever in a malaria area should be tested before treatment

Young children get sick often, and most illnesses get better. The skill you need is to tell the difference between a child you can care for at home **while staying in touch with a health worker**, and a child who must go to a facility **now**. This lesson covers three common problems: diarrhoea, fever and cough. It does not teach treatment with medicines; those decisions belong to a health worker.
Signs that mean go now

Whatever the illness, take a child to a facility immediately if the child: **cannot drink or breastfeed**, **has fits (convulsions)**, is **very sleepy, floppy or cannot be woken**, or is **breathing fast or with the chest pulling in**. WHO lists these among the signs of severe pneumonia and severe dehydration, and they are dangerous whatever the cause.
A face with a thermometer in its mouth
Fever is common in children, but some signs alongside it mean the child must go now.
Diarrhoea and dehydration

WHO defines diarrhoea as **three or more loose or watery stools in a day**, or more often than is normal for that person. The danger is **dehydration**: the body loses water and salts faster than they are replaced. WHO describes two levels:
Level
Signs WHO describes
What to do
Some dehydration
Restless or irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, thirsty
Start ORS and go to a health worker for assessment
Severe dehydration
Very sleepy or unconscious, sunken eyes, unable to drink or drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly (2 seconds or more)
Emergency: go to a facility now

**Oral rehydration solution (ORS)** is, in WHO's words, a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar. It replaces what diarrhoea removes and costs very little. Buy ORS sachets from a pharmacy or get them at your clinic, and mix each sachet **exactly as the packet says, with clean water**. Using the wrong amount of water can make the drink unsafe or weak. Ask the health worker how much to give your child. WHO also notes that **zinc**, given by a health worker, shortens diarrhoea episodes.
Keep breastfeeding, and breastfeed more often. WHO advises more fluids and more frequent breastfeeding during illness.
Keep offering soft, favourite foods to older babies and children.
Go to a health worker if there is **blood in the stool**, if diarrhoea **goes on for many days**, or if you see signs of dehydration.
Worked example: keeping a diarrhoea log
For example, Aisha's son Sani is 14 months old. He has loose stools from Saturday morning. Aisha writes each one down with the time.
By 2 pm she has recorded 3 loose stools: 7 am, 10 am and 1:30 pm. By WHO's definition this is diarrhoea.
She has ORS sachets at home from the clinic. She mixes one exactly as the packet says, in clean water, and offers it in small sips from a cup, while continuing to breastfeed.
At 6 pm she checks for danger signs: Sani is alert, drinks eagerly, no blood in the stool, no sunken eyes.
By 9 pm the count is 6 loose stools in the day. On Sunday morning he is restless and his eyes look sunken.
Restless with sunken eyes are signs of dehydration, so she takes him to the clinic that morning, with the log and his card.
Aisha did not wait for the illness to become severe. Her written log (6 stools in about 14 hours) let the health worker understand the illness quickly.
Fever and malaria

WHO's malaria fact sheet lists fever, headache and chills as the most common early symptoms, usually starting 10 to 15 days after an infected mosquito bite. Children under five and pregnant women are among those at highest risk. WHO recommends that **every suspected case of malaria is confirmed with a test**, either a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or microscopy, **before treatment**. Many fevers are not malaria, so buying malaria medicine without a test can miss the real illness.
Test, do not guess
Take a child with fever to a health worker or facility for a malaria test. Do not buy and give antimalarials or antibiotics on your own, and never use leftover medicine from another child.
Cough and fast breathing

WHO's pneumonia fact sheet explains that a child with cough or difficult breathing who has **fast breathing or lower chest wall indrawing** (the lower chest sucks in when the child breathes in) may have pneumonia. Pneumonia needs antibiotics chosen and given by a health worker. Severe cases may show inability to feed or drink, unconsciousness, a low body temperature or fits.

Module 2 was about what to do when danger appears. This lesson is about stopping illness before it starts. Prevention is quiet work: no single day feels dramatic, but the habits add up. WHO's fact sheets on pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria all point to the same small set of habits: **vaccines, mosquito nets, handwashing with soap, safe water, breastfeeding and clean air at home**.
Vaccines: the strongest single habit

WHO's pneumonia fact sheet calls immunisation against **Hib, pneumococcus, measles and whooping cough (pertussis)** the most effective way to prevent pneumonia. Its diarrhoea fact sheet lists **rotavirus vaccination** as a prevention measure. For malaria, WHO has recommended two vaccines for children living in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission: **RTS,S/AS01** (since 2021) and **R21/Matrix-M** (since 2023). In pregnancy, WHO recommends **tetanus vaccination** for all pregnant women to protect the newborn.

Each vaccine is given at a set age, and many need more than one dose to protect fully. The schedule is set by the national programme, and it can change as new vaccines are introduced. So the most reliable guide for your child is not a poster or a WhatsApp message but **the child's own vaccination card**, filled in by the health worker.
A vaccine syringe
Each dose on the card is a step towards full protection; a missed dose leaves a gap.
The vaccination card habit
Go on the due date
Health worker records dose
Write next date
Set phone reminder
Repeat the cycle at every visit until the card is complete.
Bring the card to every clinic visit, including visits for illness.
After each dose, check that it was written on the card and ask: When is the next one?
Save the next date in your phone with a reminder two days before.
If a date is missed, go to the clinic as soon as possible and ask how to catch up. Do not wait for a campaign.
Keep the card in a plastic sleeve, and take a clear photo of it in case it is lost.
Mosquito nets

WHO advises sleeping under a mosquito net in places where malaria is present. Children under five and pregnant women are among those most at risk. A net only works if it is used every night, all year, and tucked in well. Check nets for holes, and make sure the people most at risk, the pregnant woman and the youngest children, sleep under one first. In pregnancy, malaria prevention also includes the preventive treatment offered at antenatal care.

Treat the net as protective equipment, not bedding. Hang it so it reaches the floor or can be tucked under the mattress or mat, repair small holes quickly with needle and thread, and keep it away from candles and cooking fires.
Clean hands, safe water, clean air

WHO's diarrhoea fact sheet lists safe drinking water, improved sanitation, **handwashing with soap**, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, good personal and food hygiene, and health education. The pneumonia fact sheet adds **reducing indoor air pollution** and good hygiene in crowded homes. Smoke from cooking with firewood or charcoal inside a closed room is a form of indoor air pollution, so cook in a well ventilated place and keep babies away from the smoke.
Wash hands with soap and water before preparing food, before feeding a child, and after using the toilet or cleaning a child's bottom.
Store drinking water covered, and pour it out rather than dipping cups into it.
Use a toilet or latrine, and dispose of children's stools safely.

One habit at a time
Do not try to fix everything at once. Choose the habit with the biggest risk, make it automatic for a month, then choose the next.

Sharing health information responsibly: myths, WhatsApp and the health team
Check a health message against a reliable source before sharing it
Respond kindly to common myths about pregnancy, newborns and sick children
Work alongside community health workers and clinics rather than replacing them
Protect privacy when talking or posting about someone's health

After this course, people may start asking you health questions. That is a privilege and a responsibility. Good health information can save a life; wrong information, even when shared with love, can delay care. This lesson is about how to share well: check first, speak simply, point people to health workers and protect privacy.
Check before you forward
Health messages spread fast on WhatsApp, often with no source. Before you forward or repeat one, run it through four questions:
Check a health message
Who says so?
Does WHO or a clinic agree?
Does it delay care?
Share, correct or delete
If a message cannot pass the first two checks, do not forward it.
**Who says so?** A named health organisation, such as WHO or the Federal Ministry of Health, or a health worker you know? Or an unnamed forward?
**Does a reliable source agree?** Look for the same advice on an official site, or ask at your clinic.
**Could it delay care?** Any message that says to treat danger signs at home, or to avoid the clinic, is dangerous.
**Then decide**: share it with the source, correct it kindly, or delete it.
Two people sharing information
Share what you have checked, and always point people back to a health worker.
Common beliefs and what WHO says
What people sometimes say
What WHO guidance says
A kind way to respond
Give the newborn water in hot weather
Only breast milk for the first six months, no water
Breast milk already contains the water a baby needs; feed more often in the heat.
Every fever is malaria, just buy medicine
Confirm suspected malaria with a test before treatment
Let us get a quick test at the clinic so we treat the right illness.
Four antenatal visits are enough
At least eight contacts, the first by 12 weeks
The new advice is eight contacts; each one checks blood pressure and the baby.
Rub something on the cord to dry it
Hygienic cord care; keep it clean and dry
Clean and dry is best. The nurse will say if anything is needed.

Keep breastfeeding; it helps the baby recover.
Respect, not argument

Older relatives often hold these beliefs out of love and experience. Thank them, explain the reason simply, and suggest asking the health worker together. People change more easily when they do not feel ashamed.
Working with the health team

In Nigeria, primary health care centres are often the first point of care, and **community health extension workers (CHEWs)** and other community health workers visit homes, give health education and refer people to facilities. Get to know the health workers who serve your area. Ask them what days antenatal care and immunisation run, how to reach them in an emergency and how you can help, for example by reminding mothers of vaccination dates. You support their work; you do not replace it.
Worked example: answering a WhatsApp forward
For example, a message arrives in Grace's church women's group: "Pregnant women should drink this herbal mixture every morning to prevent all complications. Forward to 10 women."
Who says so? No name, no organisation. First check failed.

Does WHO agree? WHO's antenatal guidance relies on contacts with a health worker, blood pressure checks and supplements the health worker gives. It does not say any mixture prevents all complications.
Could it delay care? Yes. A woman who trusts the mixture might ignore a headache or bleeding.

Grace replies kindly in the group: "Thank you for caring. I could not find this advice from WHO or our clinic. The safest protection is the eight antenatal contacts and going straight to the hospital with any danger sign. Please ask the nurse before taking any mixture in pregnancy."
Grace stopped the message spreading in her group without shaming the sender, and gave a clear, checked alternative.
Speaking simply
Use the words people use at home, in their own language, and explain any medical word once, for example: pre-eclampsia means dangerous high blood pressure in pregnancy.
Teach a few signs at a time, and ask the person to say them back to you.
Say what to do, not only what to fear: which facility, how to get there, what to bring.
Use pictures or your danger sign card for people who do not read easily.
Privacy and consent

Health information is personal. Do not share someone's pregnancy, illness, test results or photos without their permission, even in a prayer request. When you teach, use examples without names. If someone tells you something private, keep it private, unless their life is in danger and you need to get them help.
Know your limits

If someone asks which medicine to take or how much, the answer is always: ask the health worker or pharmacist who can examine you. Saying "I do not know, let us ask the nurse" is a strength, not a weakness.
Check who said it, whether a reliable source agrees, and whether it could delay care.
Correct myths kindly and explain the reason.
Community health workers and clinics are your partners; support, never replace them.
Never answer medicine or dose questions; refer to a health worker.
Keep other people's health information private.

Part 3: a 90-day outreach plan

Health literacy spreads person to person. A good outreach plan is small and specific: **who** you will teach, **what** you will teach, **when**, and **how you will know it worked**. Choose people who most need the information: a pregnant relative, a first-time mother, a grandmother who minds children, a husband or brother who controls transport money.
A 90-day outreach plan
Days 1 to 30: household
Days 31 to 60: relatives and neighbours
Days 61 to 90: group session
Day 90: review
Start close to home, widen gradually, then review and plan the next 90 days.
Worked example: setting and tracking targets
For example, Kemi plans her 90 days. Her household has 4 adults. She also has 6 relatives and neighbours with young children or pregnancies, and her women's group of 15 meets monthly.
Days 1 to 30: teach all 4 adults at home the danger sign card. Target: 4 people.
Days 31 to 60: visit the 6 relatives and neighbours, 2 per week for 3 weeks. Target: 6 people.
Days 61 to 90: one 20-minute session at the women's group, if the leader agrees. Target: 15 people.
Total target: 4 + 6 + 15 = 25 people.
Check: after each conversation, ask the person to name three danger signs. Count it as success only if they can.
At day 90 she has reached 21 people, and 18 could name three signs. 18 / 21 is about 86%.
Kemi reached 21 of her 25 target, and about 86% of them could name three danger signs. She notes that two neighbours travelled, and adds them to the next 90-day plan.
Stay within your role
In outreach you share danger signs, plans and where to get care. You do not examine, diagnose, sell medicines or advise doses. Invite a community health worker to your group session if you can.
Part 4: the first ten minutes of an emergency

Put a short emergency script at the very top of your plan. In a real emergency people panic and forget long documents, so the first page should tell anyone in the house exactly what to do, in order, in a few lines.
Recognise: is this a danger sign on our list? If unsure, treat it as one.
Call the driver on the plan; if there is no answer within a few minutes, call the second number.
Call the facility to say you are coming and what the problem is.
Pick up the bag, the antenatal or child health card, the phone and charger, and the money.
Go to the facility that can handle emergencies, with the companion named in the plan.

Practise the script once with your household, like a fire drill. Time how long it takes to call the driver, gather the card and money and be at the door. If it takes too long, find out why: perhaps the card is in a drawer nobody can open, or the money is with someone who is away. Fix it now, while there is no emergency.

Why this matters
Most maternal deaths are preventable
Over 700 women die every day
Five complications cause about 75%
Severe bleeding, mostly after birth
Infection and high blood pressure
First week: riskiest time for a newborn
WHO, the World Health Organization, estimates that over 700 women die every day from causes linked to pregnancy and childbirth. WHO says most are preventable.
Five complications cause about 75% of maternal deaths.
The biggest is severe bleeding, mostly after the baby is born.
Others are infections, high blood pressure, problems during delivery, and unsafe abortion.
For newborns, about 75% of deaths happen in the first week of life.
Three delays, and how to cut them
Nobody knows the sign, or the family waits for permission. Knowing the signs cuts this delay.
No car at night, no fare. A written plan for transport and money cuts this delay.
No records, so staff start from zero. Carry the antenatal card every time.

When a woman dies from something treatable, time was usually lost. First, deciding at home. For example, Ngozi is 34 weeks pregnant with a severe headache and blurry eyes. Her sister says sleep, and she waits for her husband's permission.
Second, getting there. At 10 pm the usual driver does not answer.
Third, at the facility. She arrives at midnight without her card.
Each delay was avoidable: know the sign, agree in advance she can go, save a second driver's number, and keep the card in her bag.
Antenatal care
WHO: at least eight contacts
Missed a visit? Go as soon as you can. Late is better than never.
First contact in the first 12 weeks
Then 20 and 26 weeks
Then 30 and 34 weeks
Then 36, 38 and 40 weeks
Antenatal care is the care a woman gets from a skilled health worker during pregnancy. WHO recommends at least eight contacts.
The first should be in the first 12 weeks, so the early scan can be planned and iron and folic acid start early.
Then at 20 and 26 weeks.
Then 30 and 34 weeks.
Then every two weeks in the last month, at 36, 38 and 40 weeks. Put the dates in your phone. If the clinic gives a different date, follow the clinic.
And if you miss a visit, go as soon as you can. Do not feel ashamed to return.

At each contact your blood pressure is checked, and you may get iron and folic acid, a scan, a tetanus vaccine and malaria prevention. The health worker decides the product and amount.
Take your card and ask what your results mean.
Never buy pregnancy medicines on your own, and never copy what a friend was given.
Go now, day or night
Any heavy bleeding
Pain high in the belly
Fever or feeling very unwell
Any fit or convulsion
Each of these danger signs means go to a health facility now. Heavy bleeding, at any time. A severe headache that does not go away, or blurred vision, after 20 weeks. Pain high in the belly.
Fever or feeling very unwell, especially after birth. And any fit, which is an emergency.
Headache, blurred vision and upper belly pain can warn of pre-eclampsia, dangerously high blood pressure. If unsure, treat it as danger and go.
Danger sign means go now
Danger sign: go to a facility now. Do not wait.
Do not wait to see if it gets better
No herbs or medicines on the way
Choose a facility that handles emergencies
Bring the antenatal card
Call the facility on the way
For example, Amaka is 30 weeks pregnant. She has had a bad headache all day and blurry eyes, and asks her neighbour Blessing if she should just lie down.
Blessing does not suggest any medicine. She says: these are danger signs, you need your blood pressure checked tonight.
Choose a facility that can manage emergencies, such as a general hospital. Ask at antenatal care which hospital your clinic sends emergencies to.
Bring the card, and call ahead if you can. Blessing did not diagnose or treat. She removed the delay at home.
Emergency
Keep her away from fire, water and sharp objects.
Lie her on her side once the fit allows. Do not put anything in her mouth.
Get her to a facility immediately. Eclampsia needs treatment only a facility can give.
If a woman is having a fit, keep her away from fire, water and sharp objects.
And get her to a facility immediately.
After birth, watch the new mother's mind too. If she cannot cope or speaks about harming herself or the baby, she needs a health worker quickly. This is a health problem, not a weakness.

Why this matters
Plans save time when it counts
Labour often starts at night
Most newborn deaths: first week
Know when a sick child must go now
This video does not replace a health worker
Labour often starts at night, or when the person you rely on is away. Families who decide in advance save precious time.
Most newborn deaths happen in the first week, so the checks after birth matter.
And you will learn to tell a child you can care for at home from a child who must go to a facility now.
This video does not replace a health worker, and it gives no medicine doses. Those decisions belong to a health worker.
Birth and emergency plan
Five parts, written on one page
Place, and a back-up hospital
Companion and who can decide
Transport, day and night
Card and bag by the door from week 36
A birth and emergency plan answers five questions. Where will the baby be born, and which bigger hospital for an emergency? WHO says all births should have a skilled attendant.
Who goes with the mother, and who can decide to leave if her husband is away?
Who will drive, day and night? Save two numbers, and a second option.
How much will it cost? Ask the facility, not the market.
And keep the card and the bag by the door from week 36. Plan for at least 24 hours in the facility after birth. Share the plan with two people.

The first hour
Essential newborn care
Warmth: dry, skin-to-skin, covered
Breastfeed within one hour
Only breast milk for six months
Nothing on the cord: keep it clean, dry
Babies lose heat very quickly. Dry the baby and place them skin-to-skin on the mother's chest, covered with a cloth.
Start breastfeeding within one hour of birth. The thick yellowish first milk is good for the baby.
Give only breast milk for the first six months. No water, no glucose water, no herbal drinks.
Keep the cord stump clean and dry. Ash, oil or any home mixture can bring infection.
After birth
Postnatal checks in six weeks
If the clinic gives different dates, follow the clinic.
At least 24 hours in the facility
Check at 48 to 72 hours
Check at 7 to 14 days
Check in week six
WHO recommends at least 24 hours in the facility after birth, then three more checks in six weeks. For example, Chioma gave birth on Tuesday 14 July.
Her first check is due 16 or 17 July.
The next is between 21 and 28 July.
And the week six check is due around 25 August. They write the dates on the baby's card and in both phones.
Not feeding well, or stopped feeding
Very sleepy, floppy, or not moving
Difficult breathing
Fever, or the baby feels cold
A newborn with any of these signs goes to a facility today. Do not wait for the next check.
Keep the baby warm against the mother's skin, keep offering the breast, and bring the card. No herbal mixtures, glucose water or medicines on the way.
And watch the mother too. Heavy bleeding, fever, severe headache or fits mean go now.
The sick child
Home care with a health worker, or go now?
Go now
Cannot drink or breastfeed
Very sleepy, floppy, cannot wake
Fast breathing or chest pulling in
Home care and clinic
Alert and drinking
Keep breastfeeding, more often

Check for go-now signs first, every time. Cannot drink or breastfeed, fits, very sleepy or floppy, or breathing fast with the chest pulling in. Any one of these means go to a facility now.
If there are none, care at home while you see a health worker. Keep breastfeeding more often, and write down the stools, fevers and drinks.
Three common illnesses
Diarrhoea, fever and cough
3 or more loose stools a day. Mix ORS exactly as the packet says; ask the health worker how much.
Get a malaria test before treatment. Many fevers are not malaria.
Fast breathing or chest pulling in: go now. Medicines come from a health worker.

Diarrhoea is 3 or more loose or watery stools in a day. The danger is dehydration. Mix ORS, oral rehydration solution, exactly as the packet says, with clean water, and ask the health worker how much to give.
Sunken eyes or restlessness mean go to a health worker. Very sleepy or unable to drink means go now.
For fever, WHO recommends a malaria test before treatment. Never give leftover medicine from another child.
For cough with fast breathing or the lower chest sucking in, go now. Antibiotics are chosen by a health worker.

Module 2 was about what to do when danger appears. This module is about stopping illness before it starts. Small habits add up.
People may start asking you health questions. You will learn to share well.
And you will bring everything together into one family health action plan.
Remember, this video supports a health worker. It never replaces one, and it never gives medicine doses.
Vaccines
The card is your guide
Missed a dose? Go to the clinic and ask how to catch up.
Bring the card to every visit
Check each dose is written down
Ask: when is the next one?
Save the date with a reminder
Photograph the card
WHO calls vaccines the most effective way to prevent pneumonia. Your guide is not a poster or a WhatsApp message. It is the child's own vaccination card. Bring it to every visit.
After each dose, check it was written on the card, and ask when the next one is due.
Keep the card in a plastic sleeve and photograph it. And if a date is missed, go to the clinic as soon as possible. Do not wait for a campaign.
Everyday habits
Nets, clean hands, safe water, clean air
Net every night, all year, tucked in
Pregnant woman and youngest under a net first
Wash hands with soap and water
Store drinking water covered
Keep cooking smoke away from babies
Where malaria is present, sleep under a mosquito net every night, all year, tucked in well.
The pregnant woman and the youngest children sleep under one first.
Wash hands with soap before preparing food or feeding a child, and after the toilet or cleaning a child's bottom.
Store drinking water covered, and pour it out rather than dipping cups in.
And cook in a well ventilated place. Smoke from firewood or charcoal in a closed room harms children.

For example, Funmi uses an 8-point checklist and gives 1 point for each habit fully in place.

Four checks for any health message
If it says treat danger signs at home, it is dangerous.
Does WHO or your clinic agree?
Could it delay care?
Share, correct kindly, or delete
For example, Grace's church group gets a forward: pregnant women should drink a herbal mixture every morning to prevent all complications. Who says so? No name, no organisation.
Does WHO agree? WHO relies on antenatal contacts and blood pressure checks, not a mixture.
Grace replies kindly: thank you for caring, but the safest protection is the eight antenatal contacts, and going to the hospital with any danger sign.
Myths, kindly corrected
What people say, what WHO says
People say

WHO says

Older relatives often hold these beliefs out of love and experience. Thank them, and do not argue.
Explain the reason simply, and suggest asking the health worker together.
If someone asks which medicine or how much, the answer is always: ask the health worker. And never share someone's health news without permission.

Emergency script
The first ten minutes
Danger sign: go to a facility now. If unsure, treat it as one.
Recognise: is it on our list?
Call the driver, then the second number
Call the facility to say you are coming
Bag, card, phone, charger, money

Step one. Is this a danger sign on our list? If unsure, treat it as one.
Call the driver, and if there is no answer within a few minutes, call the second number. Then call the facility to say you are coming.
Pick up the bag, the card, phone, charger and money, and go to the facility that can handle emergencies.
Practise it once with your household, like a fire drill, and fix whatever slows you down.
